claim: A practitioner built a 'cron layer' gateway daemon (named OpenClaw) that manages scheduled AI-agent jobs, each defined by a Schedule (cron expression/interval/one-shot), a Payload (prompt injected as a system event or full agent turn), and a Session target (shared main session vs. isolated session).
stance_target: continuous autonomous agent operation requires an explicit scheduling/orchestration layer distinct from the agent's reasoning model
scope_conditions: single-practitioner production system, South Florida, as of 2026
quoted_support: My setup uses a gateway daemon (OpenClaw) that manages cron jobs pointing at an AI agent. Each job has three parts: Schedule... Payload... Session target — main session (shared context) or isolated (standalone).

claim: Running multiple unrelated cron-triggered agent tasks in one shared session caused context contamination: a prospect-finding job that accumulated 200+ lead records in context caused a subsequent blog-writing job in the same session to hallucinate fabricated business details.
stance_target: context isolation (separate sessions per triggered task) is necessary to prevent cross-task hallucination in continuously-running agent systems
scope_conditions: single-practitioner system, documented failure and fix, 2026
quoted_support: The prospect finder would burn through context window with 200+ lead records, then the blog writer would hallucinate about dentists in Fort Lauderdale... Isolated sessions solve this. Each cron job spins up fresh, does its work, and reports back.

claim: In an automated prospecting system, 40-60% of search results on any given run were duplicates already present in a 237-record queue, making deduplication logic (checking phone numbers and business names) the most critical component for avoiding wasted outreach at scale.
stance_target: autonomous agent loops operating continuously need built-in deduplication/state-checking logic, not just scheduling, to avoid wasted or redundant work
quoted_support: My system now has 237 prospects in the queue. On any given search, 40-60% of results are duplicates we already have... The agent checks phone numbers and business names against the existing queue before adding anything.
